demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

Negative Appraisals.value: My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper
The event happened because of the way I acted
I should have protected others and I failed

issues.item: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: For trauma involving the unexpected death of a loved one, contamination appraisals are clinically atypical and hard to reconcile unless there was a specific disgust/violation element to the death exposure. The other selected appraisals ('Bad Coper' and 'Self-Comparison') fit bereavement-related PTSD more plausibly, but 'Contamination' points toward a different trauma phenomenology (e.g., assault or abuse) and is not coherent with the provided trauma type/profile.

issues.item: Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation
issues.explanation: For trauma type 'unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one,' these two appraisals imply substantial personal responsibility for causing or entering the traumatic situation. That is hard to reconcile with an unexpected death unless there are special circumstances not reflected anywhere else in the profile. A clinician would question whether these items fit this trauma type as stated.

vignette:
Fatima Al-Rashidi is a seventy-five-year-old Jordanian-American woman who has spent more than three decades on the bench, presiding over cases with a composure that colleagues describe as almost architectural in its solidity. She came to the United States in her late twenties, built a legal career through years of disciplined effort, and raised a family in the northern Virginia suburb where she still lives with her husband of forty-eight years. It was in that same suburb, on an unremarkable Tuesday evening eleven months ago, that her youngest son, Tariq, died of a sudden cardiac event at the age of forty-four. He had been sitting at her kitchen table.

Fatima had noticed, over the preceding months, that Tariq looked tired. He had gained weight, complained occasionally of indigestion, and seemed short of breath after climbing stairs. She had mentioned it once, lightly, and he had deflected with the easy humor she had always loved in him. She did not press. She told herself he was busy, that he was a grown man, that she did not want to be the kind of mother who hovered. That evening, while she was refilling his tea, he said something she did not catch, and when she turned around he was slumped forward. By the time the paramedics arrived, there was nothing to be done.

In the months that followed, Fatima continued to appear in court each morning, robed and composed, because the alternative - the admission that she could not function - felt to her like a confirmation of something she was not yet willing to name. But the courtroom had become its own kind of ordeal. The sound of someone clearing their throat with effort, the sight of a middle-aged man loosening his collar in the heat of the gallery, the particular stillness that falls over a room when someone pauses unexpectedly - each of these had become unbearable. She would find herself gripping the edge of the bench, certain for a half-second that she was watching something begin to go wrong, that she was about to fail again to stop it.

She had come to believe, with a certainty she could not argue herself out of, that Tariq's death was her fault. Not in a vague, generalised sense, but in a specific, evidentiary one - the kind of reasoning she had spent a career applying to others. She had seen the signs. She had chosen not to act on them. A woman of her training and intelligence, she told herself, should have known better. She should have insisted he see a cardiologist. She should have said something more than once. What frightened her most was not the grief itself but the conclusion she had drawn from her own inaction: that when it mattered most, she had been exactly the wrong kind of person to have in the room.

This belief had settled alongside another, equally immovable: that the way she had responded since his death - the sleeplessness, the moments of frozen panic on the bench, the evenings she spent sitting in the kitchen unable to eat - proved something damning about her character. She had presided over cases involving trauma survivors and had always, she now admitted to herself with some shame, assumed a kind of internal toughness in herself that would hold. Its absence felt like exposure. She was certain that she was coping badly, and she read each difficult day as further evidence of that.

Her husband, Samir, had grown quietly alarmed. He had noticed her flinching at sounds, her reluctance to have family dinners in the kitchen, her habit of checking on him in the middle of the night. Their conversations had narrowed. She had not told him the full weight of what she carried, because she had come to believe it was her burden to carry alone - the consequence, as she saw it, of her own failure.

What finally brought her to seek help was a morning in court when she had to excuse herself from the bench, the first time in thirty-one years. She sat in her chambers afterward and understood that something had to change. She arrived at the intake appointment hoping, above all, to understand whether she deserved to feel this way - and afraid, in equal measure, that the answer might be yes.
